prose: This overview separates formal repetition from interpersonal recursion. The red return closes the sixteen-bar loop. Dashed connections propose that a changed horn delivery affects accompaniment and that the resulting context informs later delivery. They summarize an analytical possibility; the local graphs locate specific supporting events. Diamonds name performance variables, not documented internal deliberations.

title: 2:28–2:45 • A piano rhythm is taken up and transformed
code:
flowchart TD
 A["2:28 Hancock: ascending quarter-note triplets"] --> B{"Williams: retain time pattern or adopt triplets?"}
 B --> C["2:33 Quarter-note triplets on toms"]
 C --> D{"Repeat the adopted figure or transform it?"}
 D --> E["2:36 Five-note figure on eighth-note-triplet grid"]
 E --> F["Toms phrase undergoes diminution"]
 F --> G["2:45 Rimshot in melodic gap; clearer swing returns"]
 G --> H["Horns give B-flat a stronger attack"]
 A -. "Uptake" .-> C
 G -. "Response" .-> H
 H -. "Changed horn energy becomes new input for Williams" .-> B
prose: This is the strongest current example of a recursive exchange: piano introduces material, drums adopt and transform it, and drum punctuation is followed by changed horn delivery. The quarter-note triplets form a brief polymetric layer: continual, regular durations set against the prevailing grid for no more than a few bars. Fleeting as such layers are, they show how other metrical groupings within the existing grid can be expressive and offer ideas that others take up in turn. The dashed return represents a renewed input to subsequent drum choices, not a claim that time runs backward or that a further response has already been identified. Hearing the rimshot as reassurance is Goldford’s interpretation.

G.label: 2:45 Rimshot in melodic gap; clearer swing returns

prose: Hancock’s right-hand 7–3–13 voicing at 2:10 creates the blues sound that initiates the entire passage of exchanges. Goldford hears a correspondence between trumpet’s vocal, blues-associated inflection and piano’s semitone dissonances. This is not literal melodic imitation: a quality is proposed to migrate between timbre and harmony. The return arrow is a model of ongoing responsiveness; the subsequent piano answer still needs identification. Chord alterations and pitches await transcription.
sources: Goldford observations at 2:10 and 2:17; harmony labels provisional.
